questions: What are the giant slabs of rock that make up the crust called?
Which way are the two plates drifting - apart or towards each other?
segments.say: Two giant plates of rock sit apart. Look at Plate A and Plate B: the Earth's crust is made of giant slabs of rock called plates, and year after year they drift towards each other. Keep your student notes open at the plate and crust definitions for this scene.

questions: What happens when the two plates meet head-on?
What do the arrows in this scene show?
segments.say: The plates push together. Watch the push arrows as the drift becomes a collision: the two plates meet head-on and something has to give. Now try the collision questions on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: Which plate slides underneath - the lighter one or the denser one?
What is the special word for one plate sinking under another?
segments.say: One plate slides under the other. Watch the denser plate dive below the lighter one: that sinking is called subduction, the key word for this lesson. Check this against the subduction definition in your student notes before we move on.

questions: About how far does a plate move in one year?
Why can nobody feel a plate moving?
segments.say: Plates creep, they never lurch. Watch the marker on the plate: in a whole year it travels only about two centimetres, slower than your fingernails grow. Then finish by taking the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly the sudden-jump trap from this scene.
segments.watchFor: Plates lurch in sudden jolts, snapping into new positions. Listen and look for it in pair talk and on the exit ticket: A sudden jolt is easier to picture than a creep no one can feel. Send them back to scene s4 and to the correct turn: Plates creep, they never lurch: about two centimetres a year, slower than your fingernails grow.

title: Plate tectonics: giant slabs on the move
